content: Adequate nutrition plays a critical role in maintaining optimal immune and metabolic function. For individuals living with HIV, dietary support may help improve clinical outcomes by reducing the occurrence of HIV-related complications, slowing the progression of the disease, enhancing quality of life, and ultimately decreasing disease-related mortality. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of various macronutrient interventions, administered orally, in reducing morbidity and mortality among adults and children with HIV infection. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and Gateway, covering studies up to 2012. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed, and authors of pertinent studies were contacted. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared the effects of macronutrient interventions with either no nutritional supplementation or placebo in managing HIV-infected adults and children. Three independent reviewers applied selection criteria, evaluated study quality, and extracted data. The effects of interventions were analyzed using mean differences and 95% confidence intervals. Where appropriate, data from homogenous studies were pooled, and meta-analyses were performed using a random-effects model. Fourteen trials were included in the review, involving 1,725 HIV-positive adults and 271 HIV-positive children. The findings revealed that neither supplementary food nor daily Spirulina supplementation significantly reduced the risk of death compared to no supplementation or placebo in malnourished, antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naive adults. Similarly, in children with prolonged diarrhea, a nutritional supplement enhanced with protein did not significantly alter the risk of death compared to standard nutritional care. However, supplementation with macronutrient formulas designed to provide protein and/or energy, fortified with micronutrients, and combined with nutrition counseling significantly improved energy intake (mean difference of 393.57 kcal/day; 95% CI: 224.66 to 562.47; p < 0.00001) and protein intake (mean difference of 23.5 g/day; 95% CI: 12.68 to 34.01; p < 0.00001) in adult participants experiencing weight loss. These results were based on three trials for energy intake (n=131) and two trials for protein intake (n=81). In general, supplementation with specific macronutrients, such as amino acids, whey protein concentrate, or Spirulina, did not result in significant improvements in clinical, anthropometric, or immunological outcomes when compared to placebo in HIV-infected adults and children. The authors concluded that the current evidence base, derived from fourteen relatively small trials, is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the effects of macronutrient supplementation on morbidity and mortality in people living with HIV. The studies included in the review evaluated different macronutrient supplements in diverse populations at varying stages of HIV infection and treatment status. Despite these limitations, it is encouraging to see an increasing number of studies being conducted in low-income countries and among children, where macronutrient supplementation, both before and during antiretroviral treatment, may hold potential benefits.
